scenes.narration: Code is read far more often than it is written. Today we learn two ways to explain a function to its readers.

scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A docstring is a string placed on the first line of a function body. It says what the function does. Type hints show the type of each parameter, after a colon, and the type of the result, after an arrow. Think of a label on a spice jar. It tells you what is inside. But it does not stop you pouring something else in. Python reads hints, but does not enforce them. Tools like editors use them to warn you.

scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] Each parameter has a colon and a type. The arrow, and float, say the result is a float. [HL 2] The docstring, in triple quotes. It must be the first thing in the body. [HL 3] The code itself. [HL 4] Two and a half times four is ten point zero. [HL 5] Every function keeps its docstring in a special attribute. Printing it shows the text. Editors show this text when you hover over the function.

code.source:
def area(width: float, height: float) -> float:
    """Return the area of a rectangle."""
    return width * height
print(area(2.5, 4))
print(area.__doc__)

scenes.narration: [HL 1] A string parameter, and an int parameter with a default of one. The result is a string. [HL 2] A one line docstring. [HL 3] Repeat the greeting. [HL 4] Greeting Asha twice, with the spaces trimmed. [HL 5] Python stores the hints in a dictionary on the function. Tools can read it. But Python itself never checks them while the program runs.

code.source:
def greet(name: str, times: int = 1) -> str:
    """Greet a person, repeated times times."""
    return ("Hi " + name + ". ") * times
print(greet("Asha", 2).strip())
print(greet.__annotations__)

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: hints do not stop wrong types
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The hint says n is an int. We pass the string ab. Python does not complain. It repeats the string, and prints abab. Type hints are labels, not locks. If a wrong type must be rejected, check it yourself inside the function. Editors and tools also read the hints, and can warn you before you run.

props.why: Type hints are notes for people and tools; Python still runs the code with any type, so add a check yourself if a wrong type must be rejected.

shorts.title: Docstrings
shorts.hook: "A docstring is a string on the first line of a function body."
shorts.script: A docstring is a string on the first line of a function body. It says what the function does, in one short sentence. Use triple quotes. Python keeps the docstring on the function, and editors show it when you hover. Write one for every function that is not obvious. You and your team read it before they read the code. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Explain your function.

shorts.title: Type hints
shorts.hook: "Type hints show what a function expects."
shorts.script: Type hints show what a function expects. After each parameter, a colon and a type. After the brackets, an arrow and the type of the result. Def area, width colon float, arrow float. A reader sees at once what goes in and what comes out. Editors use hints to warn you about mistakes before you even run the program. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Say what goes in.

shorts.title: Hints are notes
shorts.hook: "Here is the truth about type hints."
shorts.script: Here is the truth about type hints. Python does not enforce them. They are notes for people and tools. You can pass a string to a parameter marked int. Python still tries to run the code. If you need a wrong type to be rejected, check it yourself. Hints help you write better code, but they are not a lock. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Notes, not locks.

shorts.title: Abab
shorts.script: A surprising bug. The hint says n is an int. You pass the string ab. Python does not complain, and prints abab, because a string times two repeats the text. Hints are labels, not locks. Use an editor that reads hints, or check types yourself when it matters. Never assume that a hint stops a wrong value from arriving. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Python does not check.
